2.text: “Possibly a council-room, as well as a theatre,” says he, “for in place of the

3.text: usual inner arrangements, only a species of bench of raised earth ran around

4.text: it, where were seated numerous spectators.”¹ No remembrance of such public

5.text: tents, however, is retained at Uñiˊsak. Perhaps it was simply a private house

6.text: in the course of partial reconstruction, as often happens with native houses.

7.text: It may have been used temporarily by the people for a re-union on the oc-

8.text: casion of the arrival of the author.

9.text: The ceremonials of different families, though performed at the same

10.text: place, were rarely observed in common. On the contrary, families enacted

11.text: their ceremonials one after another, even though each particular performance

12.text: lasted for several days. Even at present, though the ceremonials are per-

13.text: formed by each family in their own house, the consecutive order is still fol-

14.text: lowed, and thus the winter ceremonial in the largest villages often extends

15.text: over a month or even more. As a partial corrective, three or four families

16.text: perform on the same day; but in this case they usually belong to opposite

17.text: ends of the village, with separate circles of acquaintances and relatives.

18.text: The hunting of sea-mammals is not forbidden during this whole period.

19.text: The members of the house actually performing the ceremonial must, of course,

20.text: stay at home; but as soon as it is over, the family has a right to send some

21.text: of their people to the sea, even though others go to take part in a ceremo-

22.text: nial feast of some of their “neighbors.”

23.text: Sacrifice to the Sea. — The sacrifice to the sea, which, together with the

24.text: sacrifice to the dead, begins the cycle of the Maritime ceremonials, is per-

25.text: formed by the best hunter of the family. He comes to the shore accom-

26.text: panied by one woman. He carries his harpoon and other weapons; while

27.text: she brings a vessel filled with blood-soup and sausage of reindeer-stomach.

28.text: This sausage plays as important a part in the sacrifices of the Maritime

29.text: people as it does among the reindeer-breeders. The Maritime people are

30.text: more inclined to select “alien food” for their sacrifices than are the reindeer-

31.text: breeders. The products of civilization, such as sugar or flour (thanks to the

32.text: trading activity of whalers), do not appeal to them as rare dainties: therefore

33.text: they give the first place, in sacrificing, to the products of the reindeer-breeders,

34.text: which are their conception of what is most luscious.

35.text: While the woman brings the sacrifice, the man shows his weapons to

36.text: the sea, and asks for good luck in hunting and for safety in his future wan-

37.text: dering over the unstable ice-floes. A dog is often slaughtered in sacrifice to

38.text: the sea. The time of this sacrifice differs in different families. Some perform

39.text: it at the end of summer; others, on the contrary, delay it till the middle of

40.text: October, when it coincides with the moving from the summer tents to the

41.text: winter habitations. Connected with the sacrifice to the sea there is often
